content: Randomized controlled trials would provide stronger evidence to support the implementation of point-of-care (PoC) RNA assays. Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant global public health issue and a leading cause of liver disease, with a disproportionately high burden in lowand middle-income countries. In 2019, an estimated 58 million people were chronically infected with HCV, and approximately 290,000 HCV-related deaths occurred. In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) introduced its first Global Health Sector Strategy for Viral Hepatitis (2016–2021), aiming to eliminate hepatitis B and C by 2030 through expanded prevention, testing, and treatment interventions. Progress has been made, including simplified diagnostic and treatment pathways and increased access to affordable, short-course generic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens. The 2018 WHO guidelines on chronic HCV care and treatment recommended good-practice approaches to simplify service delivery through decentralization, integration, task-shifting, and improved access to effective hepatitis services. A recent WHO-led systematic review has provided robust evidence supporting these approaches in HCV care. Full decentralization of HCV testing and treatment at the same site, compared to partial or no decentralization, has been associated with improved linkage to care and treatment uptake, particularly among people who inject drugs. However, as of 2019, only 21% of individuals with chronic HCV had been diagnosed, and less than 25% of those infected had received treatment. To meet the 2030 targets of diagnosing 90% of cases and treating 80% of those infected, a significant scale-up of testing and treatment is required. The 2017 WHO viral hepatitis testing guidelines recommend an initial screening for HCV infection using an HCV antibody serological assay (either a rapid diagnostic test or a laboratory-based immunoassay), followed by laboratory-based nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA to confirm viremia and determine the need for treatment. HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) testing was conditionally recommended as an alternative. Despite widespread access to low-cost DAA treatments, the requirement for confirmatory HCV viral load (VL) testing for antibody-positive individuals—often associated with high costs—can result in significant patient attrition across the care cascade. Currently, laboratory-based HCV RNA NAT is the standard-of-care assay for HCV VL testing. These technologies are highly sensitive and specific for detecting viremia and allow for high-throughput testing in centralized laboratories. However, they require laboratory infrastructure, highly trained personnel, and are less accessible in resource-limited settings. PoC NAT assays, which can be used at or near the site of patient care, are increasingly being adopted as an alternative testing approach. Several commercially available PoC RNA assays now exist. These devices are often battery-operated, do not require continuous electricity, use reagents that can be stored at ambient temperatures, and can provide results within two hours using fingerstick or whole blood samples. This enables same-day clinical decision-making. PoC devices are simpler to use than laboratory-based NAT assays and can improve access to HCV viremia diagnosis and treatment monitoring, particularly in populations with high rates of loss to follow-up, such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, migrants, and rural communities. These devices also enable same-day diagnosis of HCV viremia (alone or combined with HCV antibody testing) and can be used for test-of-cure purposes. While high-quality evidence exists for the use of PoC assays in improving uptake and reducing time to results and treatment initiation for HIV viral load monitoring, early infant diagnosis, and tuberculosis, data on their impact on HCV VL testing and treatment access remain limited. The 2017 WHO testing guidelines emphasized the need to evaluate the impact of PoC NAT tests on HCV viremia testing access compared to conventional laboratory-based testing to inform updated guidelines. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to assess the impact of PoC HCV VL testing compared to centralized laboratory-based approaches on HCV RNA testing uptake, treatment initiation, and turnaround time to treatment among HCV antibody-positive individuals. Outcomes were evaluated across population subgroups, including people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, prisoners, people living with HIV, and general or mixed populations. Models of care were categorized based on whether PoC HCV VL testing was performed at the clinic site or a remote site and further stratified by the timing and location of testing and treatment. Understanding the impact of PoC NAT testing versus conventional laboratory-based NAT testing on HCV viremia diagnosis uptake will help inform updated WHO testing guidelines. The primary research question focused on whether PoC HCV VL testing increases HCV RNA testing and treatment uptake and reduces time to treatment initiation compared to standard laboratory-based approaches. Secondary questions explored the differential effects of PoC testing in specific care models and populations with poor access to care and high loss-to-follow-up rates, such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, migrants, and people living with HIV. The systematic review included studies using PoC HCV RNA assays with data on HCV care cascade outcomes and/or turnaround times. Studies were included if they reported at least two adjacent steps in the HCV care cascade, enabling calculation of proportions. Data on time intervals between care cascade stages were also included. Studies with a sample size of 10 or fewer were excluded. Data were extracted and analyzed to assess the impact of PoC testing on key outcomes, including HCV RNA testing uptake, treatment initiation, and time to treatment. The analysis revealed that PoC devices, particularly those used on-site or in mobile units, can significantly reduce turnaround times and improve care cascade outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of PoC HCV VL testing to address barriers in HCV care, especially in resource-limited settings and among marginalized populations. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to strengthen the evidence base and guide the implementation of PoC RNA assays in diverse healthcare settings.
